title: Creation: Bill Callahan talks about his latest release 'Gold Record' with Lauren and Simon on Breaking and Entering
summary: American singer-songwriter Bill Callahan contemplates family, cars, nostalgia and his new album Gold Record with Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler on Breaking and Entering. He muses on the topic of how creating a family is similar to creating artistic works: "it's kind of paying tribute to creation when we create".
transcript:
Bill Callahan spoke with Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler from the balcony of his home in Austin, Texas, for an interview broadcast on Breaking and Entering on 17 September 2020. They discussed Gold Record, songwriting, family and the connections between its characters. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Bill was in the country earlier in the year, back in March, and performed at Golden Plains. I imagine that would have been one of the last gigs he played before COVID hit and we all went into lockdown. His new album, Gold Record, came out earlier this month. Woke on a Whaleheart, released nearly 13 years ago, was the first record he recorded under his own name after switching from his Smog moniker.

Simon: For those coming to Bill Callahan’s music more recently, he is a deeply beloved songwriter, guitarist and recording artist who performed under the name Smog, pioneering a sound of lo-fi underground rock with homemade tape albums recorded on four-track recorders. He later released albums with Drag City, to which he remains signed decades later. Shepherd in a Sheepskin Vest was his return last year, following Dream River in 2013. His first live album, Rough Travel for a Rare Thing, was recorded in 2007 at the Toff in Melbourne. There’s a strong connection to this city, where he played six shows at Howler on his last tour before his recent appearance at Meredith, too.

Lauren: Gold Record came together quickly, recorded in a week, with half the tracks recorded in one take and the rest in no more than two. The last record was very focused on Bill himself; on this one he wanted to focus on the stories and perspectives of others. He starts the new record introducing himself as Johnny Cash and ends as Leonard Cohen. It also features a reworking of the Smog track ‘Let’s Move to the Country’, originally recorded 20 years ago. Bill released a song every Monday for nine weeks, inviting an audience to spend a little more time with each before moving on. As a listener, is this how you like to engage with music, a little more slowly and deliberately?

Bill: I think with the way that music is distributed these days, streaming is the major source for the way people listen to things. When you go on one of those sites and there’s a million songs, it can be a little hard to focus on one song, or ten songs, one album or anything like that. So really I was just trying to make a way that people could focus. Also, knowing that everybody’s in the same boat right now, pretty much. Some people have nicer boats than others. But just a way to give myself and other people something to look forward to for nine weeks.

Lauren: It’s been that for sure, which we’re very grateful for. A statement around Gold Record describes it as your warmest, wittiest and most comforting work. While these aren’t your words, do you ever intend for a song to bring warmth or comfort to yourself or to others?

Bill: I think that’s why people listen to music, for comfort, or something energising, something soothing, an escape or a fantasy. I take into account all those things.

Simon: These songs have been described as self-contained short stories and character studies. Listening to Gold Record has been likened to reading a collection of stories by authors like Raymond Carver. We read that a significant portion of these songs arose while you were reviewing old notebooks. Can you tell us about that process and how the songs took shape?

Bill: Some of the songs were started as long as ten years ago. Obviously, ‘Let’s Move to the Country’ was written 20 years ago. About five of them were written in the last couple of years. I didn’t really have the impetus to finish them because I tend to work on songs in batches. I tend to write an album at a time, so anything that’s not fitting into the current album plan gets pushed aside. I had a few songs that just weren’t fitting in. The concept of Gold Record is ten songs that don’t fit in, but they do fit in with each other by the fact that they are standalone songs that aren’t very interrelated to each other.

Simon: In unexpected ways they become their own connecting narrative. In ‘Let’s Move to the Country’, sentences that were left incomplete at the time have been completed years later. How does it feel to revisit and revise a song like this?

Bill: Normally I wouldn’t dream of updating a song. For me, I only have to believe in a song long enough to get in the studio and record it. For that time period, I have to think it’s a great song and I couldn’t do better. But once it’s released, the veneer fades. You start seeing how something might have been better. I wouldn’t tend to go and try to correct that song. I’ll just say, let me start from scratch with a different song. But with ‘Let’s Move to the Country’, I think it was probably my only song that was completely set up for revision because it had incomplete sentences. It’s a very specific song about having kids. It’s a quantifiable song, but a lot of people seem to like it. I didn’t really think people would care one way or the other, but a lot of people are appreciating the new version for some reason, which is good.

Simon: There are so many ways of interpreting and responding to each of the songs. As you were listening intensively during mixing and recording, were there any unexpected connecting threads or things you found emerging that unified the record to you?

Bill: Actually, there is. There’s a lot, beyond the fact that there’s a guy named Jack in two of the songs, who I’m pretty sure is the same guy. He’s the guy that invites the narrator inside his house, and then it gets revealed that Jack has lost his son. But he’s also at the wedding in ‘Pigeons’, trying to give a speech and crying too much to finish it. Maybe he’s crying because his own son didn’t make it to get married. He died before he could experience that. There’s little things like that. I also feel like a lot of the record seems to be set in the ’70s for some reason. It seems like a very ’70s record to me, ’70s in America. It wasn’t intentional at all, but it just happened.

Simon: There were currents of change and profound social shifts occurring at that time. Is there something subconscious you feel reflected in present-day America?

Bill: I’m not really nostalgic for anything at all, but maybe watching TV in the past is something I’m nostalgic for. I love in movies when someone’s watching a black-and-white TV. For some reason, to watch a movie of someone watching TV is very comforting and familiar to me. Maybe because I watched so much TV when I was a kid.

Lauren: There are references to Sesame Street on your last record as well. I often find myself in a YouTube spiral watching all the ’70s Sesame Street videos. Were you the same?

Bill: No, I watch new ones with my son. I think Sesame Street is a pretty current type of show. I think it’s important to watch the current Sesame Street.

Simon: Television was fresh in those decades, and there were shows that everybody had as common reference points. In the fragmented online space, maybe people don’t have that same sense of watching or experiencing the same thing simultaneously.

Bill: Now television is so personalised, and there’s a channel for everything. You can get your smart TV and pick the channels you want, and you don’t even have to skip past the channels you don’t want. They’re just not there anymore. There’s something to be said for TV being something that maybe isn’t that good, but you’re forced to watch it because that’s all there is. I knew all that TV I was watching in the ’70s and ’80s was complete trash, but I didn’t care. Even news, now you just watch the news station that says what you believe, how you feel, which is dangerous. The reporters are gearing their report to what you want to hear so that you keep watching. It’s become a lot more biased.

Lauren: You’ve mentioned that songwriters like Johnny Cash and Leonard Cohen are among those you see as parental figures or role models. Parenthood was at the heart of Shepherd in a Sheepskin Vest. How is that relationship, that parenthood dynamic, reflected on Gold Record?

Bill: It’s just the way that I see the world, really. Right now I can see two birds on my front yard. I’m assuming that they’re man and wife and they probably have some kids. I just see all relationships in that way, maybe because family is the first thing that we know, the first relationship we know. I think it extends to ‘The Mackenzies’, where the guy who is being treated like a son is a father himself. Everybody is a daughter or a mother and a father and a son.

Lauren: You’ve said that for many people there’s a strong desire to be a parent to something, whether a person, an animal or a creative pursuit. Could you tell us about that impulse in yourself and what you’re discovering about your philosophies on parenting?

Bill: Having a child is an extreme act of creativity, but so is making a clay jar and painting it. I think that when we create, it’s the most spiritual thing, and we’re mimicking the creation of the world, no matter what we’re creating. It’s paying tribute to creation when we create. It just seems like what we were born to do.

Simon: In interviews around Shepherd, you talked about briefly imagining leaving songwriting to focus on family. Did you come back to songwriting with a renewed understanding of its place in your life?

Bill: That lasted about a week, when I thought maybe I’ll just be a full-time dad. Sleep deprivation makes you think crazy things. My wife was like, ‘Hell no.’ Like, ‘I fell in love with the guy that writes the songs.’ She wanted him to stay alive, so she quickly talked some sense into me.

Simon: The car features in some of your lyrics, including as the spark of the first interaction in ‘The Mackenzies’. There’s also a car on the cover of Gold Record. It’s a potent symbol in American history, and the road trip has a special place in the collective consciousness. Could you tell us about the vehicle and its place on this record?

Bill: I love cars, even though I know that they are evil as far as the environment. But I think they’re a wonderful invention. As far as the cover image, I was looking for a 21st-century noir type of feel. I don’t listen to my music after it’s released, but I listen to it a lot while I’m mixing it, and I listen a lot while I’m driving. It seems to be the best place, for me at least, to listen to my music. My wife said she thinks it’s the perfect road trip album, and a few other people have said that to me too. It has a wide-open sound. There’s a lot of space in there to allow you to think.

Lauren: There’s playfulness in the title Gold Record and your promo photos, a reference to gold-selling albums, 500,000 copies sold and champagne flowing. The title also raises the question of what constitutes success and what’s truly meaningful or valuable. What makes an album or a song successful to you?

Bill: To me, a record is a success if you actually go through the process of writing it and recording it and designing a cover and the liner notes and all that. To me that’s the ultimate success. I’ve felt that way from day one, when I released my first album. I made 200 copies, and I had no idea how to distribute them or get any kind of notice, get the word spread or sell them. But I didn’t really care. I just had these amazing two boxes, or it was like four boxes, of 200 records in my closet, and I was happy as a clam. It’s still the same with me. I’ve been doing it for a long time, and some of my records sell more than others, and it doesn’t really matter because I always know I’m going to make another one. I’ve always looked at the big picture, right from when I made my first album in 1990. I just had a sense that this is what I was going to do for the rest of my life, and however I could get by and do that was all that I needed to feel worthwhile.

Simon: In your recent chat with Cheryl Waters from KEXP, one subject was balance and how you’ve enjoyed the yin and yang of touring and home life, getting away but also wishing to be home. In 2020 that balance has been redrawn profoundly. Can you describe the new equilibrium of your time and days?

Bill: Although sometimes it feels like the world is ending, this country is ending, there’ll be a new beginning, I hope, for the world and this country and all the other countries. But I think you still just have to take care of yourself, exercise and socialise in whatever prophylactic manner is necessary. Although all those things that enrich you may seem more difficult or more hopeless, just keep that balance of doing those things.
